docs.title: Your computer
docs.text: Needed Windows Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit (x86-64). Windows on ARM (for example Snapdragon laptops) is not supported: the installer stops on its first screen. RAM 8 GB (16 GB recommended) Free disk space about 10 GB, for the install and the models it downloads on first use Internet while installing, and on the first run of each model WebView2 Microsoft Edge WebView2 Runtime, for the GUI (the installer offers it if it is missing)

docs.title: Your graphics card
docs.text:
The installer makes this install for one accelerator (see Accelerated or not):

  • An NVIDIA GPU that 1.10 supports — GTX 16 series, RTX 20 series or newer, with driver 580 or newer: the install is made for the NVIDIA GPU (CUDA) by itself, without a question.
  • Anything else — an AMD or Intel graphics card, an NVIDIA card older than 1.10 supports, an older driver, or no graphics card WhisperJAV can use: a window asks what the install should be made for.

To check your NVIDIA driver version, right-click the desktop, open the NVIDIA Control Panel and look at "Driver Version" in the bottom-left corner. To update it: nvidia.com/drivers, then restart the PC.

docs.title: Antivirus
docs.text: Some antivirus programs block the installer's downloads. If that happens, add an exclusion for %LOCALAPPDATA%\WhisperJAV, or pause real-time scanning while installing.

docs.title: Users in China
docs.text: The installer downloads from GitHub, PyPI, download.pytorch.org and Hugging Face. Keep your VPN on during the whole installation.

docs.title: Installation steps
docs.text:
1. Download WhisperJAV-1.10.2-Windows-x86_64.exe from the releases page.
  2. Double-click it. You do not need to run it as administrator. If Windows SmartScreen warns, click More info, then Run anyway.
  3. Accept the licence.
  4. Choose Just Me (recommended; no administrator rights) or All Users.
  5. Choose the folder. The default is C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Local\WhisperJAV. Keep the path short, and avoid spaces if you can.
  6. Click Install.

After the files are unpacked, a console window runs the rest of the installation. It shows each phase:

Phase What happens 1 Checks: free disk space, the connection to PyPI, the Visual C++ runtime, WebView2 2 Looks for an NVIDIA GPU and its driver 2.5 Decides what the install is made for; shows the window when it has to ask (see below) 3–4.5 Installs the package versions this release was tested with, then PyTorch for that accelerator 5 Installs WhisperJAV 5.1 NVIDIA GPU (CUDA) install only: places the CUDA 12 library balanced, fast and faster need; if this PC cannot load it, installs the CUDA 12.8 build of PyTorch instead 5.5–5.8 Creates the WhisperJAV-GUI.exe launcher, downloads the FireRedVAD speech detection model, checks the icons 6 Checks that the installed program starts

At the end, a summary shows what was installed and what the install is made for, and a desktop shortcut "WhisperJAV v1.10.2" and a WhisperJAV entry in the Start menu are created. The installation takes about 10 to 30 minutes, depending on your connection.

docs.title: What this install is made for
A supported NVIDIA GPU
docs.text: No question is asked. The install is made for the NVIDIA GPU (CUDA 13.0). If this PC cannot load the CUDA 12 library that balanced, fast and faster need, the installer says so in a framed message and installs the CUDA 12.8 build instead.

docs.title: No supported NVIDIA GPU: the window
docs.text:
When the installer finds no NVIDIA GPU that 1.10 supports, a window titled "WhisperJAV — no supported NVIDIA GPU found" asks:

WhisperJAV found no NVIDIA graphics card that version 1.10 supports (graphics found: …). What should this install be made for?

Choice The install is made for AMD graphics card GPU through Vulkan Intel graphics card GPU through Vulkan NVIDIA graphics card older than WhisperJAV 1.10 supports GPU through Vulkan I have my own PyTorch for my GPU (advanced) Own PyTorch None, or use the CPU only CPU only (not accelerated)

The window explains:

With an AMD, Intel or older NVIDIA card, the GGUF pipelines (run by CrispASR) ask for your graphics card through Vulkan. This is experimental: it has not been tested on AMD or Intel graphics cards, and we would like to hear how it works for you. All other pipelines run on the CPU (not accelerated), several times slower than on a supported NVIDIA GPU. With your own PyTorch, WhisperJAV installs everything except PyTorch, and you add your PyTorch build afterwards (the command is shown at the end). With the CPU only, every pipeline runs on the CPU.

Without an answer, the CPU-only version is installed after 20 seconds. Stop ends the installer without installing anything.

GPU through Vulkan needs the Vulkan runtime (vulkan-1.dll), which comes with your graphics driver. If it is missing, the installer says so and installs the CPU-only version; update the graphics driver and run the installer again to change that.

docs.title: An NVIDIA GPU that 1.10 cannot use
docs.text:
The window starts with the reason, and Stop is pre-selected, with no time limit:

  • An older card (below GTX 16 / RTX 20): "Your graphics card, … (compute capability …), is older than WhisperJAV 1.10 supports. 1.10 needs a GTX 16-series, RTX 20-series or newer card." and "WhisperJAV 1.9.5 still supports this card: https://github.com/meizhong986/WhisperJAV/releases/tag/v1.9.5." If you are sure the card is supported, My card is identified wrongly shows where to report it, then stops.
  • An older driver (below 580): "Your NVIDIA driver (…) is older than WhisperJAV 1.10 needs (580 or newer). Update it from https://www.nvidia.com/drivers, restart the PC, and run this installer again to get the NVIDIA GPU version. Or choose below."
  • A card Windows lists but WhisperJAV cannot reach — the driver may be missing or not working, or, on a laptop with two graphics chips, the NVIDIA chip may be switched off: install or repair the NVIDIA driver (580 or newer), restart the PC and run the installer again. Or choose below.

docs.title: Own PyTorch
docs.text:
WhisperJAV installs everything except PyTorch, and never installs, replaces or removes PyTorch in this install at install or upgrade. Running the installer again replaces the whole install folder, PyTorch included: the window keeps Own PyTorch and shows the command again. At the end, a window shows the one command to run, with WhisperJAV's Python filled in:

"<install folder>\python.exe" -m pip install torch torchaudio --index-url <the address of your PyTorch build>

PyTorch 2.11 is recommended. The same command is saved in <install folder>\OWN_PYTORCH_NEXT_STEP.txt. Until you have run it, every WhisperJAV run stops at its start and shows the command again.

docs.title: Where the install's choice is kept
docs.text: The installer writes the accelerator into whisperjav_stack.txt in the install folder. Every run, whisperjav-upgrade and every later run of the installer follow it.

docs.title: When the installer stops on purpose
docs.text: If you choose Stop, a closing dialog says: "WhisperJAV was not installed. The installer stopped for the reason shown in its console window." The reason is also saved in INSTALLATION_STOPPED_v1.10.2.txt in the install folder.

docs.title: First run
docs.text:
Double-click the WhisperJAV v1.10.2 shortcut, choose WhisperJAV in the Start menu, or double-click WhisperJAV-GUI.exe in the install folder.

The first time a pipeline needs a model, WhisperJAV downloads it (for example about 3 GB for Whisper large-v3, 674 MB for Parakeet-CrispASR). Later runs reuse it.

At the start of each run, WhisperJAV checks the install:

  • NVIDIA GPU (CUDA) install, GPU usable: nothing is shown; the run goes on.
  • NVIDIA GPU (CUDA) install, GPU not usable now (for example after a driver change): the run does not start. A box names the reason and the fix. To run on the CPU this time, add --device cpu; in the GUI, the dialog "The NVIDIA GPU cannot be used" offers Run on the CPU this time.
  • Every other install: a box says what the install is made for and where each part runs on this computer, then the run goes on.

Basic workflow: add files, choose a mode (Balanced is a good start), click Start. The subtitles are written to the output folder you chose.

docs.title: Checking your installation
docs.text:
Open a Command Prompt (press Start, type cmd, press Enter) and run:

cd /d "%LOCALAPPDATA%\WhisperJAV"
Scripts\whisperjav.exe --check

(Use your install folder if you chose another one.)

It lists WhisperJAV's version, Python, PyTorch and where it is loaded from, the accelerator of the install, where each part runs, FFmpeg, CrispASR and the models, and whether the addresses that installs and downloads need answer. On an NVIDIA GPU (CUDA) install, for example:

✓ PyTorch: PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130: NVIDIA GPU (CUDA 13.0), NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060
✓ CrispASR: 0.8.53+cuda (CUDA build), GGUF pipelines: asks for the NVIDIA GPU (CUDA)
ℹ Accelerator: Accelerator of this install: NVIDIA GPU (CUDA 13.0).
ℹ CTranslate2: CTranslate2 (balanced, fast, faster): NVIDIA GPU (CUDA)

Scripts\whisperjav.exe --version prints the version: WhisperJAV 1.10.2.

The installation log is install_log_v1.10.2.txt in the install folder.

docs.title: Coming from 1.9.x
docs.text: Install the newest 1.10 release fresh: 1.10 needs Python 3.13, so whisperjav-upgrade cannot take a 1.9.x install to 1.10. If you install into the folder of your old version, the installer finds it and offers to replace it: everything in that folder is removed first. Your settings in %APPDATA%\WhisperJAV and your downloaded models stay.

docs.title: Updating within 1.10
docs.text:
Later 1.10 releases are installed with WhisperJAV's upgrade tool, which keeps the accelerator of your install and its PyTorch. The GUI tells you when a new version is out, but it does not upgrade by itself.

  1. Close WhisperJAV.
  2. Open a Command Prompt.
  3. Run "%LOCALAPPDATA%\WhisperJAV\python.exe" -m whisperjav.upgrade (or the python.exe in your install folder) and answer y.
  4. Check the version: "%LOCALAPPDATA%\WhisperJAV\Scripts\whisperjav.exe" --version (or Scripts\whisperjav.exe in your install folder)

Start the upgrade with the install's python.exe, not with Scripts\whisperjav-upgrade.exe: when WhisperJAV is installed on another drive than Windows' temporary folder (normally drive C:), whisperjav-upgrade.exe of 1.10.0, 1.10.1 and 1.10.2 stops halfway and WhisperJAV no longer starts. If that happens, or WhisperJAV does not start after an upgrade for another reason, uninstall it and install the newest release with the installer; your settings and downloaded models stay.

Do not update with a plain pip install -U whisperjav…: on Windows, PyPI serves the CPU-only build of PyTorch, so it can replace your GPU build without a word.

docs.title: Running the installer again
docs.text: Run the installer again into the same folder to repair the install or to change what it is made for. A window titled "WhisperJAV — this install's accelerator" says "This install is made for: …. Keep it, or choose another." The current accelerator is pre-selected; without an answer, the install is kept as it is after 20 seconds. If the NVIDIA GPU cannot be used at that moment, the reason is shown above the choice. The installer removes the old install folder first (your settings and downloaded models stay) and keeps only its record of the accelerator; on an Own PyTorch install, add your PyTorch again with the command shown at the end. If WhisperJAV no longer starts, for example after a failed upgrade, uninstall it first and then install it again.

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text: Open Windows Settings > Apps, find WhisperJAV and choose Uninstall. On an install made with the 1.10.2 installer, the uninstall also removes this install's desktop shortcut and its Start-menu entry; an install made with an earlier installer and then upgraded keeps that installer's uninstaller, which leaves them. The downloaded models stay in %USERPROFILE%\.cache (Hugging Face and Whisper caches) and your settings in %APPDATA%\WhisperJAV; delete those folders by hand to free the space.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
"No supported NVIDIA GPU found" although you have an NVIDIA card. Read the first line of the window: it names the reason (old card, old driver, or a card WhisperJAV cannot reach). Update or repair the driver, restart the PC and run the installer again. On a laptop with two graphics chips, make sure the NVIDIA chip is switched on.

The run stops: "THE NVIDIA GPU CANNOT BE USED". The install is made for the NVIDIA GPU, and the GPU cannot be used now. The box names the reason and the fix. --device cpu runs that one job on the CPU.

Processing is slow. Look at the box at the start of the run, or run whisperjav --check: they say where each part runs. On a CPU-only install, every pipeline runs on the CPU, several times slower than on a GPU.

The GGUF pipelines stop: "CrispASR could not be loaded". With the GPU-through-Vulkan or Own PyTorch install, this usually means the Vulkan runtime (vulkan-1.dll) is missing: update the graphics driver, or run the installer again and choose CPU only.

Downloads fail or time out. Check the connection; behind a firewall, allow python.exe, uv.exe and git.exe. The installer retries GitHub downloads with longer timeouts. In China, keep your VPN on for the whole installation.

The GUI does not open, or the window is blank. Install WebView2 from Microsoft. To see error messages, run "%LOCALAPPDATA%\WhisperJAV\python.exe" -m whisperjav.webview_gui.main in a Command Prompt.

The installation failed. Open install_log_v1.10.2.txt in the install folder: it names the phase that failed. INSTALLATION_FAILED_v1.10.2.txt holds the reason. Run the installer again; it offers to replace the partial install. If it keeps failing, open an issue at GitHub Issues with the log attached.

docs.title: Silent installation
docs.text:
cmd /C START /WAIT WhisperJAV-1.10.2-Windows-x86_64.exe /S /D=C:\WhisperJAV

/S installs without the installer's screens; /D= sets the folder and must come last. WhisperJAV-1.10.2-Windows-x86_64.exe /? lists every option. The window of What this install is made for still opens when the installer has to ask: on a PC without a supported NVIDIA GPU it installs the CPU-only version after 20 seconds without an answer; with an NVIDIA GPU that 1.10 cannot use, it waits for an answer.

docs.title: Files in the install folder
docs.text: File What it is install_log_v1.10.2.txt the installation log whisperjav_stack.txt what the install is made for OWN_PYTORCH_NEXT_STEP.txt Own PyTorch install only: the command that adds your PyTorch INSTALLATION_STOPPED_v1.10.2.txt only when the installer stopped on purpose: the reason INSTALLATION_FAILED_v1.10.2.txt only when the installation failed: the reason WhisperJAV-GUI.exe the GUI launcher

docs.title: Addresses the installer downloads from
docs.text: Address For pypi.org, files.pythonhosted.org Python packages download.pytorch.org PyTorch github.com CrispASR's GPU builds and packages installed from GitHub huggingface.co models (installation and first run) aka.ms, go.microsoft.com the Visual C++ runtime and WebView2, if missing

docs.title: Pipelines
docs.text: WhisperJAV offers multiple processing pipelines, each trading speed for accuracy. Choose based on your content and hardware.

docs.title: Pipeline Comparison
docs.text: Pipeline Backend Scene Detection VAD Speed Accuracy GPU Memory Faster Faster-Whisper No No Fastest Good ~2 GB Fast Whisper Yes No Fast Better ~4 GB Balanced Whisper Yes Yes Medium Best (Whisper) ~4 GB Fidelity Whisper Yes Full Slow Maximum ~6 GB Transformers HuggingFace Yes Yes Medium Good ~4 GB Qwen3-ASR Qwen3 Assembly Assembly Medium Excellent text ~4-8 GB ChronosJAV anime-whisper / Kotoba TEN VAD TEN VAD Medium Best for anime/JAV ~4-8 GB GGUF pipelines: parakeet, cohere, reazonspeech, kotoba, whisper-turbo, whisper-large, MOSS, haas, qwen3-asr (Ensemble only) CrispASR (Parakeet, Cohere, ReazonSpeech, Kotoba-Whisper, Whisper, MOSS, Haas, Qwen3-ASR models) Yes (Semantic by default) Yes (TEN VAD / FireRedVAD) Not measured Not measured Not measured

docs.title: Which Pipeline Should I Use?
docs.text: Scenario Recommended Pipeline First time, just want subtitles Balanced (default) Processing many files quickly Faster Anime or JAV content ChronosJAV with anime-whisper Maximum accuracy, don't mind waiting Ensemble: Balanced + Qwen3-ASR with Smart Merge No GPU (CPU only install) Faster Apple Silicon Mac Transformers (MPS acceleration)

docs.title: Ensemble Mode
docs.text: Run two passes with different pipelines and merge the results. See Ensemble Mode for details.

docs.title: Specialized Pipelines
docs.text:
• ChronosJAV — anime-whisper and Kotoba models for anime/JAV content
  • Qwen3-ASR — alternative ASR engine with strong Japanese text quality
  • GGUF pipelines (CrispASR) — nine pipelines, GGUF models through CrispASR, installed with WhisperJAV; Ensemble Mode, Japanese, experimental

docs.title: ChronosJAV Pipeline
docs.text:
ChronosJAV is a pipeline for anime and JAV content. It runs two kinds of ASR model: Qwen3-ASR, whose Model menu also has two Japanese fine-tunes (one tuned on game speech), and anime-whisper, made for anime and visual-novel dialogue.

Inspired by the temporal-awareness approach in ChronusOmni (Chen et al., 2025).

docs.title: Available Models
docs.text:
In the Ensemble Mode tab, the Pipeline menu's ChronosJAV group has two pipelines, Qwen3-ASR and Anime-Whisper. The pass's Model menu then offers:

Pipeline Model menu entry GPU memory, as the menu gives it Qwen3-ASR Qwen3-ASR-1.7B (the default) 8 GB Qwen3-ASR-0.6B 4 GB JA Anime-Galgame 1.7B (jaykwok's fine-tune) 8 GB JA-tuned 1.7B (neosophie) 8 GB Anime-Whisper anime-whisper (the default) ~4 GB efwkjn/whisper-ja-anime-v0.3 (experimental, #232) ~3 GB Kotoba v2.0 ~2 GB Kotoba v2.1 ~2 GB

Tip

If your graphics card has less than 8 GB of memory, choose a model the menu lists with less: Qwen3-ASR-0.6B (4 GB) or an Anime-Whisper model (2 to 4 GB).

docs.title: GUI
docs.text:
1. Open the Ensemble Mode tab (ChronosJAV is not in the Transcription Mode tab)
  2. In the Pipeline menu of Pass 1 or Pass 2, choose Qwen3-ASR or Anime-Whisper (group ChronosJAV); the pass's sensitivity and speech segmenter change to the pipeline's own
  3. Choose a model in the pass's Model menu
  4. Click Start

On the command line: whisperjav video.mp4 --mode qwen (Qwen3-ASR), or --mode qwen --qwen-generator anime-whisper.

docs.title: As Part of Ensemble
docs.text: ChronosJAV can run as Pass 1, Pass 2 or both, with any other pipeline as the other pass. With Pass 2 ticked, the two passes' subtitles are combined by the strategy chosen under Merge (default Pass 1 + Fill From Pass 2; see Merge Strategies).

docs.title: Technical Details
docs.text:
ChronosJAV uses different defaults than the standard Whisper pipelines:

Setting ChronosJAV Default Standard Default Decoding Greedy (beam=1) differs by pipeline (Balanced: beam search with 2 beams) Speech Segmenter FireRedVAD, TEN VAD or WhisperSeg, by pass (see below) differs by pipeline Timestamp Mode VAD only (since 1.10.1, as in 1.9.5; 1.10.0: Aligner + VAD fallback) the Whisper model's own times Text Cleaner Qwen3-ASR: Qwen3 AssemblyTextCleaner; anime-whisper: its own text cleaner — Clean-up after the subtitles are made ChronosJAV's own: it removes lone lines such as 「あ。」, lines made only of moaning or breathing sounds, and overlaps where two scenes meet, among other steps; no hallucination filter the sanitizer, with the hallucination filter

The speech segmenter a ChronosJAV pass starts with: in the Ensemble Mode tab, FireRedVAD for Qwen3-ASR as Pass 1, WhisperSeg for Anime-Whisper as Pass 1, and TEN VAD for either as Pass 2. On the command line: WhisperSeg for --mode qwen; in an Ensemble run the same as in the GUI. The pass's Speech Segmenter menu, --pass1-speech-segmenter / --pass2-speech-segmenter or --qwen-segmenter changes it.

docs.title: Subtitle timing
docs.text:
ChronosJAV's ASR models write text without times. Since 1.10.1, by default, Qwen3-ASR and anime-whisper subtitles take their start and end from the piece of speech (VAD group) the speech segmenter found, as in 1.9.5: no aligner and no timing model run, and neither is downloaded. Two sentences in one piece of speech — for example two speakers — come out as one subtitle.

1.10.0 timed the text by default with two more steps; since 1.10.1 they run only when chosen:

  1. The aligner times each character of the text the ASR model wrote. wav2vec2-ja (232 MB) is used when no other is named.
  2. The timing model, Whisper small (488 MB), runs on each piece of speech; its own text is not used. Where Whisper starts a new segment, the piece of speech is split into separate subtitles at the punctuation mark (such as 。？！…、 or a closing bracket) or space in the text nearest that point. Without such a mark nothing is split. No number of characters or seconds decides a cut, and no split leaves on its own a part that WhisperJAV's clean-up would then delete (such as a lone moan or a lone はい); such a part stays with its neighbour. Each subtitle starts where the aligner puts its first character and ends where the next one starts; the last one ends where the piece of speech ends. Where the aligner gave no times, the timing model moves the start later, to where Whisper hears the speech begin.

Both run in CrispASR, which is installed with WhisperJAV, and are downloaded the first time a ChronosJAV run uses them. They run where the install's CrispASR runs (see Where they run), so on a GPU-through-Vulkan or Apple GPU install they ask for the GPU (not yet tried on either) while the ASR model runs on the CPU.

Choice GUI (Customize → Alignment) Command line VAD only (default) Timestamp Mode: VAD Only (no aligner loaded) --qwen-timestamp-mode vad_only (default) Aligner Timestamp Mode: Aligner + VAD Fallback, Aligner + Interpolation or Aligner Only; then Aligner Backend: CrispASR (GGUF, recommended) or Qwen3 ForcedAligner (PyTorch), and Aligner Model --qwen-timestamp-mode aligner_vad_fallback (or aligner_interpolation, aligner_only), with --qwen-aligner wav2vec2-ja (used when none is named), qwen3-fa-gguf, parakeet-ctc-ja, or Qwen/Qwen3-ForcedAligner-0.6B. --qwen-aligner given without --qwen-timestamp-mode turns on aligner_vad_fallback Timing model Timing Model (Whisper): Whisper small, None (no timing model; default) --qwen-timing-model whisper-small, or none (default) Step-down Adaptive Step-Down (off by default; shown with an aligner mode) --qwen-stepdown (off by default)

In an Ensemble pass from the command line, the same choices go in --pass1-qwen-params, for example '{"timestamp_mode": "aligner_vad_fallback", "timing_model": "whisper-small"}' for 1.10.0's timing. An aligner_id, or an aligner_backend of crispasr or qwen3, given without timestamp_mode also turns on aligner_vad_fallback.

  • parakeet-ctc-ja is not recommended: its times came back evenly spread in our tests.
  • Without an aligner, a chosen timing model still moves each subtitle's start, but splits nothing.
  • With Subtitle Regrouping (Output tab; --qwen-regroup) set to Standard or Sentence Only instead of Off (the default), the regrouping makes the splits. In an aligner mode the start comes from the aligner, and a chosen timing model only moves the start of a piece of speech the aligner gave no times, though it still runs. With VAD Only, the regrouping divides each piece of speech's text and shares out its times by the length of the text.
  • To get ChronosJAV's times as in 1.10.0 (the aligner and the timing model): --qwen-timestamp-mode aligner_vad_fallback --qwen-timing-model whisper-small, or in the GUI Timestamp Mode Aligner + VAD Fallback and Timing Model Whisper small. A GUI preset saved from a ChronosJAV Customize window in 1.10.0 keeps the Timestamp Mode and Timing Model it was saved with; one saved with 1.10.0's defaults still runs the aligner and the timing model.
  • When something does not work, the text is kept. If the aligner cannot be loaded (for example on the first run without internet) or gives no times for a piece of speech, those subtitles are not split and take the times of their pieces of speech; the timing model may still move their start. If the timing model cannot be loaded, nothing is split and the times come from the aligner. The run summary says which part and why.
  • With Aligner + VAD Fallback and the other settings at their defaults, if the aligner piles the words of a scene together (the collapse check), that scene's subtitles take the times of their pieces of speech and are not split; a chosen timing model moves their start. Step-down, which instead retries such a scene with pieces of speech up to 6 seconds long, is off by default.
  • With --device cpu, the aligner and the timing model, when chosen, cannot be held on the CPU: where CrispASR's build uses a GPU, they still ask for it, and the box at the start of the run says so. On a computer without a GPU they run on the CPU; how long the timing model takes there has not been measured.
  • 1.10.0's timing (the aligner and the timing model), measured on 7 scenes of The Naked Director against Netflix's Japanese subtitles: subtitles starting within 0.5 s, Qwen3-ASR 78% (1.9.5: 75%), anime-whisper 77% (1.9.5: 63%); the text scores the same as 1.9.5. A typical subtitle still starts about 0.06 to 0.09 s after the reference; 1.9.5's, which timed each subtitle by its piece of speech as the 1.10.1 default does, started slightly before it; the 1.10.1 default has not been measured.

docs.title: First Run
docs.text:
On first use, the model is downloaded from HuggingFace (~2-4 GB depending on model). This is a one-time download — subsequent runs use the cached model. The aligner (232 MB) and the timing model (488 MB) are downloaded only when a run chooses them (since 1.10.1; 1.10.0 downloaded both on its first ChronosJAV run), at the start of that run, before any audio is read; if the download fails, the run stops (since 1.10.2).

Models are cached in your HuggingFace cache directory:

  • Windows: C:\Users\<you>\.cache\huggingface\
  • macOS/Linux: ~/.cache/huggingface/

docs.title: GGUF pipelines (CrispASR)
docs.text:
There are nine GGUF pipelines: Parakeet-CrispASR and Cohere-CrispASR; new in 1.10.1, ReazonSpeech-CrispASR, Kotoba-CrispASR, Whisper-Turbo-CrispASR, Whisper-Large-CrispASR and MOSS-CrispASR; new in 1.10.2, Haas-CrispASR and Qwen3-ASR-CrispASR. They make Japanese subtitles with ASR models in the GGUF file format (the Whisper models in whisper.cpp's format). They run through CrispASR, which is installed with WhisperJAV in every install; there is no separate program to download.

  • Ensemble Mode only. They run as Pass 1, Pass 2 or both in the Ensemble Mode tab. They have no --mode value and are not in the Transcription Mode tab.
  • Japanese only. Any other source language stops the run with a message.
  • Experimental (early release): Parakeet-CrispASR and Cohere-CrispASR since 1.10.0, five new in 1.10.1, two new in 1.10.2. Compare their subtitles with those of the pipelines you use now, and tell us how they work for you: https://github.com/meizhong986/WhisperJAV/issues

Folder names

The GGUF (CrispASR) pipelines need folder names in plain Western letters (ASCII). When your user folder has Chinese, Japanese or Korean characters, WhisperJAV links or copies the model to a plain-named folder (the original stays where it is).

This concerns the folder that holds the model file: CrispASR is given no other path (the audio is handed to it in memory). On Windows, WhisperJAV first tries the folder's short (8.3) name; only if that is not available does it put a link or copy in C:\Users\Public\WhisperJAV\crispasr (or C:\ProgramData\WhisperJAV\crispasr), and the log says so. A copy takes up to 4.1 GB and is kept for later runs. CrispASR's CPU build, installed in a folder with Japanese characters, was checked once: it loaded the model and transcribed from there. WhisperJAV itself, and CrispASR's CUDA and Vulkan builds, have not been checked in such a folder.

Coming from 1.9.x?

The 1.9.x CrispASR mode, which ran a crispasr program you downloaded yourself, is removed. See Upgrading from 1.9.x.

docs.title: Where they run
docs.text:
Every install since 1.10.0 includes CrispASR, in the build that fits the accelerator the install is made for (see Accelerated or not):

Install made for CrispASR build The GGUF pipelines run on NVIDIA GPU (CUDA), Windows and Linux x86-64 CUDA build the NVIDIA GPU GPU through Vulkan (Windows) Vulkan build your graphics card through Vulkan — experimental, not tested Own PyTorch, Windows Vulkan build your graphics card through Vulkan — experimental, not tested Apple GPU (Metal), Apple silicon Mac macOS build asks for the Apple GPU (Metal) — not yet tested on a Mac Own PyTorch, Apple silicon Mac macOS build asks for the Apple GPU (Metal) — not yet tested on a Mac CPU only; Own PyTorch on Linux; Linux on ARM64 CPU build the CPU (not accelerated), several times slower

The processor must support AVX2 (Intel processors since 2013, AMD since 2015). Without it, the GGUF pipelines stop with a message before any audio is read; every other pipeline works.

At the start of each pass, the log says where CrispASR is asked to run, for example:

Parakeet-CrispASR asks CrispASR to use the NVIDIA GPU (CUDA) (CrispASR 0.8.53+cuda).

With the Vulkan build: "Parakeet-CrispASR asks CrispASR's Vulkan build to use this PC's GPU (CrispASR 0.8.53+vulkan). GPUs through Vulkan are experimental and have not been tested on AMD or Intel graphics cards." WhisperJAV cannot yet read which device CrispASR actually used; the line states what it asked for.

docs.title: Parakeet-CrispASR and Cohere-CrispASR
docs.text:
Parakeet-CrispASR Cohere-CrispASR Name in the GUI parakeet (under GGUF via crispasr) cohere (under GGUF via crispasr) Model parakeet-tdt-0.6b-ja (default, 674 MB) or parakeet-tdt-0.6b-ja-f16 (1,247 MB) cohere-asr-ja-v0.1 (default) or cohere-asr-ja (2,424 MB each); their full-size files cohere-asr-ja-v0.1-f16 and cohere-asr-ja-f16 (4,137 MB each) Default speech segmenter TEN VAD FireRedVAD Default sensitivity Aggressive Balanced Longest VAD group 6 s, at every sensitivity 3 s Where a subtitle ends only at a natural break in the speech (see below) only at a sentence end (see below) Subtitle times (default; the Timing tab changes it) from the model's own timing of what it wrote from the aligner wav2vec2-ja, which times the model's text Audio analytics report yes yes

A VAD group is a stretch of speech, a few seconds long, that the speech segmenter finds and hands to the model in one piece.

Parakeet-CrispASR uses the speech segmenter settings of the Fidelity pipeline, with a 6-second limit. Cohere-CrispASR uses those of the Qwen3-ASR pipeline.

docs.title: The five pipelines new in 1.10.1
docs.text:
GUI (under Experimental, open to feedback) Command line Models (default first) What it is reazonspeech reazonspeech-crispasr reazonspeech-nemo-v2-f16 (1,240 MB), reazonspeech-nemo-v2-q8_0 (667 MB) ReazonSpeech's Japanese model, reazonspeech-nemo-v2 kotoba kotoba-crispasr kotoba-whisper-v2.0-f16 (1,520 MB), kotoba-whisper-v2.0-q5_0 (538 MB) Kotoba-Whisper v2.0, a Whisper model made smaller ("distilled") for Japanese whisper-turbo whisper-turbo-crispasr whisper-large-v3-turbo-f16 (1,625 MB), whisper-large-v3-turbo-q8_0 (874 MB) OpenAI Whisper large-v3-turbo whisper-large whisper-large-crispasr whisper-large-v2-f16 (3,095 MB), whisper-large-v2-q8_0 (1,656 MB), whisper-large-v3-f16 (3,095 MB), whisper-large-v3-q5_0 (1,081 MB) OpenAI Whisper large-v2 or large-v3 MOSS moss-crispasr moss-transcribe-diarize-0.9b-f16 (1,823 MB), moss-transcribe-diarize-0.9b-q8_0 (1,410 MB) OpenMOSS's MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize 0.9B; WhisperJAV does not use its speaker labels

How they differ from the two above:

  • reazonspeech takes Parakeet-CrispASR's speech segmenter settings (TEN VAD, Aggressive, VAD groups up to 6 s). Its times come from the model, which gives each word a start only: a new subtitle starts only after a sentence end, each ends where the next starts, and the last ends where its VAD group ends.
  • kotoba, whisper-turbo and whisper-large take Cohere-CrispASR's speech segmenter settings (FireRedVAD, Balanced, VAD groups up to 3 s). Their times come from the model; a new subtitle starts only after a sentence end.
  • MOSS works on longer stretches: Semantic scenes of 90 to 240 s, and FireRedVAD (Balanced) VAD groups that end at a silence longer than 5 s and are at most 240 s. Each segment MOSS writes is one subtitle, at MOSS's own times. Its Customize Parameters window has a MOSS tab, and its clean-up differs (see How the subtitles are made).

docs.title: The two pipelines new in 1.10.2
docs.text:
GUI (under Experimental, open to feedback) Command line Models (default first) What it is haas haas-crispasr haas-ja-v1.0-f16 (1,233 MB, ~1.6 GB of GPU memory), haas-ja-v1.0-q8_0 (656 MB, ~0.9 GB) third-intelligence's Haas-ja-v1.0, a Japanese model of the Parakeet kind qwen3-asr qwen3-asr-crispasr qwen3-asr-1.7b-f16 (4,705 MB, ~6.3 GB of GPU memory) Qwen3-ASR-1.7B, the model of ChronosJAV's Qwen3-ASR, here as a GGUF file run by CrispASR instead of PyTorch

Both take Parakeet-CrispASR's speech segmenter settings (TEN VAD, Aggressive, VAD groups up to 6 s), the settings they were tested with before they were added.

  • haas is made like Parakeet-CrispASR: its times come from the model, which times every word, and a subtitle ends only at a natural break in the speech.
  • qwen3-asr is made like Cohere-CrispASR: its model gives no times, so ChronosJAV's text cleaner for Qwen3-ASR first cleans each VAD group's text (for example, it shortens a word repeated over and over), then the aligner wav2vec2-ja times it, and a subtitle ends only at a sentence end. With From the model in the Timing tab (--pass1-word-timestamps model) there is no aligner: each VAD group is one subtitle, from its start to its end. It is not part of ChronosJAV: no timing model and no ChronosJAV clean-up; it is cleaned as the other GGUF pipelines are.

docs.title: GUI
docs.text:
1. Open the Ensemble Mode tab. It opens with Pass 1 on cohere (Balanced, FireRedVAD) and Pass 2 on parakeet (Aggressive, TEN VAD); Pass 2 is off until you tick it. With Remember settings on, the tab opens on the passes you saved instead.
  2. To choose another pipeline for a pass, open its Pipeline menu: parakeet and cohere are under GGUF via crispasr; below a divider line, the seven new in 1.10.1 and 1.10.2 are under Experimental, open to feedback (reazonspeech, kotoba, whisper-turbo, whisper-large, MOSS, haas, qwen3-asr). Choosing one sets its own sensitivity, speech segmenter and scene detector, as in the tables above.
  3. Choose the model in the Model column. Each entry names the file's number format and the GPU memory it needs, for example "Parakeet TDT 0.6B ja (q8_0), ~0.9 GB VRAM"; the pipeline's default is first.
  4. If you want a second pass, tick Pass 2, check its pipeline, and choose how the two are combined under Merge.
  5. Click Start.

When a pass uses one of these pipelines:

  • Sensitivity, Speech Segmenter, Model, Scene Detector, Speech Enhancer (with its For VAD only box, ticked by default since 1.10.2) can be set, as for the other passes. None as the speech segmenter skips speech detection: each scene goes to the model whole, so silence and music reach the model too.
  • Customize Parameters opens four tabs: Segmenter, Enhancer, Scene and Timing (one menu, Word timestamps: From the model or From the aligner (wav2vec2-ja), the pipeline's default marked "(default)"); for MOSS also a MOSS tab. They start from the values the pass runs with.
  • A status panel under the pass row shows the model and where CrispASR will run, for example:
Model: Parakeet TDT 0.6B ja (q8_0) — not downloaded yet (674 MB); downloaded when the run starts
GPU: asks for the NVIDIA GPU (CUDA)

It can also show "CPU (not accelerated), several times slower: " or "CrispASR cannot run here: ". When the pass's times come from the aligner (Cohere-CrispASR's default, or From the aligner in the Timing tab), it also lists the aligner, for example "Aligner: wav2vec2 large XLSR-53 ja (q4_k) — not downloaded yet (232 MB); downloaded the first time it is used".

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
One pass:

whisperjav video.mp4 --ensemble --pass1-pipeline parakeet-crispasr

Two passes, with Cohere-CrispASR and its second model as pass 2:

whisperjav video.mp4 --ensemble --pass1-pipeline parakeet-crispasr --pass2-pipeline cohere-crispasr --pass2-model cohere-asr-ja

Without --merge-strategy, two passes are combined with pass1_primary (in the GUI: "Pass 1 + Fill From Pass 2").

docs.title: What you can set
docs.text:
Setting GUI Command line Notes Model Model --pass1-model, --pass2-model each pipeline's models, in the two tables above Speech segmenter Speech Segmenter --pass1-speech-segmenter any; none sends each scene to the model whole Sensitivity Sensitivity --pass1-sensitivity conservative, balanced, aggressive; default aggressive for Parakeet-, ReazonSpeech-, Haas- and Qwen3-ASR-CrispASR, balanced for the others Scene detector Scene Detector --pass1-scene-detector semantic (default), auditok, silero: scenes of normally 12 to 48 s, a shorter piece joined to its neighbour (MOSS-CrispASR: 90 to 240 s); none (one scene per file) Speech enhancer Speech Enhancer --pass1-speech-enhancer none (default) or the speech enhancers of the other passes, for example ffmpeg-dsp, zipenhancer or htdemucs Enhance for VAD only For VAD only (Speech Enhancer menu) --pass1-enhance-for-vad the cleaned audio goes to the speech segmenter only; CrispASR hears the original Detection threshold Customize, Segmenter tab --pass1-vad-threshold 0 to 1; replaces the value the sensitivity sets Padding Customize, Segmenter tab --pass1-speech-pad-ms milliseconds added before and after each piece of speech. Cohere-, Kotoba-, Whisper-Turbo- and Whisper-Large-CrispASR: both sides. Parakeet-, ReazonSpeech-, Haas- and Qwen3-ASR-CrispASR: only with a speech segmenter that has padding, such as WhisperSeg; with FireRedVAD or TEN VAD it is ignored, with a warning. MOSS-CrispASR: only with a speech segmenter that has padding Subtitle times Customize, Timing tab: Word timestamps --pass1-word-timestamps model or aligner default aligner for Cohere-CrispASR and Qwen3-ASR-CrispASR, model for the others (MOSS-CrispASR: its own segment times). With aligner, a VAD group the aligner times is cut as Cohere-CrispASR's are (see below); a group it gives no times keeps the pipeline's own rule MOSS settings Customize, MOSS tab (MOSS-CrispASR only) keys in --pass1-params Instruction language, Language hint, Hotwords, Token limit per piece, Sampling, Temperature, Top-k, Seed, Beam size (1 to 4); the keys are listed in --help under --pass1-params Device — --device auto, cuda or cpu see below Language Source audio language --language japanese (default) any other language stops the run

(The same flags exist for pass 2: --pass2-….)

docs.title: Sensitivity
docs.text:
Sensitivity picks the speech segmenter's preset. Aggressive accepts sound the speech segmenter is less sure is speech; Conservative accepts only sound it is surer of. With the default speech segmenters:

Conservative Balanced Aggressive Parakeet-CrispASR (TEN VAD): detection threshold 0.42 0.32 0.22 Parakeet-CrispASR: padding before / after speech 0 / 300 ms 0 / 200 ms 0 / 100 ms Cohere-CrispASR (FireRedVAD): detection threshold 0.5 0.4 0.3 Cohere-CrispASR: padding before and after speech 100 ms 100 ms 100 ms

The detection threshold is how sure the speech segmenter must be that a sound is speech, from 0 to 1. ReazonSpeech-, Haas- and Qwen3-ASR-CrispASR take Parakeet-CrispASR's values; Kotoba-, Whisper-Turbo- and Whisper-Large-CrispASR take Cohere-CrispASR's. The longest VAD group stays 6 s (Parakeet-, ReazonSpeech-, Haas-, Qwen3-ASR-CrispASR), 3 s (Cohere-, Kotoba-, Whisper-Turbo-, Whisper-Large-CrispASR) or 240 s (MOSS-CrispASR) at every sensitivity. With another speech segmenter, each pipeline uses the values the Fidelity pipeline (for Parakeet-, ReazonSpeech-, Haas- and Qwen3-ASR-CrispASR) or the Qwen3-ASR pipeline (for the others but MOSS-CrispASR) gives it; the 6-second limit stays.

To see the values a run will use, without running it:

whisperjav --ensemble --pass1-pipeline parakeet-crispasr --dump-params settings.json

and look under crispasr_effective in settings.json.

docs.title: Device
docs.text:
• --device auto (the default, and what the GUI uses): the GPU the install's CrispASR build can use (see Where they run), otherwise the CPU. The log says which, and why.
  • --device cuda: requires the CUDA build and an NVIDIA GPU it can use; otherwise the run stops before any audio is read.
  • --device cpu: always the CPU for the ASR model. In the GUI, "Run on the CPU this time" does the same for one run. The aligner (Cohere-CrispASR's default, or any pass set to From the aligner) cannot be held on the CPU: where CrispASR's build uses a GPU it still asks for it, and the box at the start of the run says so.

--device governs every pipeline of the run, the speech enhancer included.

docs.title: Not used by these pipelines
docs.text:
• If you give --pass1-hf-params or --pass1-qwen-params, one log line names them ("Parakeet-CrispASR does not use: …") and the run goes on.
  • --compute-type is ignored, with a warning: each model file has its own number format (f16, q8_0 and others); choose the file with --pass1-model.
  • --subs-language direct-to-english still gives Japanese subtitles, with a warning. Translate them afterwards with --translate or whisperjav-translate.

docs.title: How the subtitles are made
docs.text:
For each video, every GGUF pipeline:

  1. extract the audio (16 kHz, mono; 48 kHz when a speech enhancer is chosen, which then gives 16 kHz audio);
  2. divide it into scenes with the scene detector (Semantic, 12 to 48 seconds, by default; MOSS-CrispASR 90 to 240 seconds);
  3. clean the audio of each scene, if a speech enhancer is chosen; the enhancer is closed before the model opens, so the two never hold GPU memory together;
  4. run the speech segmenter on each scene and put the speech it finds into VAD groups;
  5. send each VAD group to the model on its own; without a speech enhancer the model is loaded once per pass, with one it is opened for each video's ASR step and closed after it;
  6. make subtitles from each VAD group's text, by the pipeline's rule below;
  7. join the scenes and clean the subtitles. All but MOSS-CrispASR first run the Fidelity pipeline's merge of repeated lines, its hallucination filter and its repetition cleaner, then the three filters of the Qwen3-ASR pipeline: they remove lone lines such as 「あ。」 or 「うん。」, lines made only of moaning or breathing sounds, and duplicates and overlaps where two scenes meet. MOSS-CrispASR runs the merge of repeated lines and the three filters, then removes lines made only of ああ, あっ, うん or えっ, and lines without kana that are one interjection such as "Oh" or 啊. A copy of the subtitles before the clean-up, and a list of what it removed or changed, are kept in the raw_subs folder beside the pass's subtitle file (<name>.pass<N>.<pipeline>_stitched.original.srt and .artifacts.srt);
  8. write the pass's subtitle file, which Ensemble Mode combines with the other pass's when there is one.

Parakeet-CrispASR: where a subtitle ends. Within a VAD group, a new subtitle starts only at a natural break:

  • after a sentence-end mark (。 ？ ！ … and the like);
  • at a pause of at least 0.6 seconds;
  • at a 、 or a space followed by a pause of at least 0.4 seconds.

It never cuts by number of characters or by length in seconds, so speech with no such break stays one subtitle, as long as its VAD group (up to about 6 seconds). Each subtitle starts where its first word starts and ends where its last spoken word ends, from the times the model gives.

Cohere-CrispASR: a subtitle ends at a sentence end. After Cohere writes a VAD group's text, the aligner wav2vec2-ja (run by CrispASR) finds when each character of that text is spoken. Within the VAD group, a new subtitle starts only after a sentence-end mark of the text (。 ？ ！ … ? !); a number such as 3.5 is never cut. Each subtitle starts at its first spoken character and ends where the next one starts; the last ends at the end of the VAD group. Pauses do not cut here: the aligner gives the moment each character starts, not where a sound ends, so a held sound would look like a pause. VAD groups are at most 3 seconds, or about 4.2 seconds when one stretch of speech runs on without a break.

If the aligner gives no times for a VAD group, that group stays one subtitle from where the speech segmenter found the speech start to where it found it end, and the run summary counts such groups. If the aligner cannot be loaded at all (for example on the first run without internet), every group is made that way and the run summary says so; the text is kept in both cases. New in 1.10.0; not yet measured against reference subtitles.

Audio analytics. As the Qwen3-ASR pipeline does, every GGUF pipeline prints a short report for each video: which parts may lose speech and which are acoustically hard, with their times, so you can check those places. The report needs the Semantic scene detector; with another one, a log line says so and no report is made.

docs.title: The model download
docs.text:
• WhisperJAV downloads the model the first time a pipeline needs it, at the start of the run, before any audio is read. It checks first that there is enough free disk space (the model's size plus 10 %).
  • The models come from Hugging Face:
Model Hugging Face repository File parakeet-tdt-0.6b-ja cstr/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-ja-GGUF parakeet-tdt-0.6b-ja-q8_0.gguf cohere-asr-ja-v0.1 TransWithAI/cohere-transcribe-ja-v0.1-GGUF cohere-asr-ja-v0.1-q8_0.gguf cohere-asr-ja CKHO/cohere-asr-ja-GGUF cohere-asr-ja-q8_0.gguf aligner wav2vec2-ja (Cohere-CrispASR by default, any GGUF pass set to From the aligner, and ChronosJAV's aligner modes when no other aligner is named) cstr/wav2vec2-large-xlsr-53-japanese-GGUF wav2vec2-large-xlsr-53-japanese-q4_k.gguf

The aligner (232 MB; Cohere-CrispASR's default, and any pass set to From the aligner) is downloaded the first time a pass uses it, inside the pass, not before the run. If that download fails, the pass goes on without it: each VAD group becomes one subtitle at the group's edges (see How the subtitles are made). ChronosJAV's other aligners and its timing model are listed in whisperjav --check and on the ChronosJAV page.

  • The file is kept in your Hugging Face cache folder (by default C:\Users\<you>\.cache\huggingface\ on Windows, ~/.cache/huggingface/ on macOS and Linux) and reused by later runs.
  • Before first use, WhisperJAV checks the file against the version it expects. A damaged download is deleted and downloaded once more.
  • If huggingface.co cannot be reached, WhisperJAV tries the mirror hf-mirror.com, as it does for its other models. --hf-endpoint <address> names another mirror.
  • With --offline (GUI: "Offline mode (downloaded Hugging Face models only)") nothing is downloaded. If the model is missing, the run stops before transcribing and says so; run once without --offline first.
  • If the download or the check fails, the run stops with "CrispASR is not ready for this run" and the reason. Nothing is transcribed.

Using a model file you downloaded yourself. Put the file, with its name unchanged, in a plain-named folder and set the environment variable WHISPERJAV_CRISPASR_MODEL_DIR to that folder. WhisperJAV uses the file only if it has the expected size, and checks it before first use. A file that fails the check stops the run and is not deleted.
